subject: Chemistry
text: Mohan has three solutions P, Q and R having a pH of 13, 5 and 2 respectively. Which of the above solutions P, Q or R: (a) will react with Magnesium to liberate hydrogen gas? (b) will liberate ammonia gas when it reacts with ammonium chloride?
modelAnswer: (a) Solutions Q (pH 5) and R (pH 2) are acidic and both will react with Magnesium to liberate hydrogen gas. R (pH 2) is more strongly acidic. (b) Solution P (pH 13) is strongly alkaline (NaOH type) and will react with ammonium chloride to liberate ammonia gas.
keyPoints: Acids (pH < 7) react with Mg to give H2
Strong alkalis react with NH4Cl to give NH3
P=alkaline, Q=weakly acidic, R=strongly acidic

subject: Chemistry
text: The following table is related to an Industrial process of an acid. Name of the process | Reactant | Catalyst | Final product. Identify: (a) the name of the process (b) the catalyst used (c) the final product, given the reactant is SO2 + O2.
modelAnswer: (a) Contact Process (b) Vanadium Pentoxide (V2O5) (c) Sulphuric acid (H2SO4). In the Contact Process, SO2 + ½O2 → SO3 (with V2O5 catalyst), then SO3 is absorbed in H2SO4 to form oleum, which is diluted to give H2SO4.
keyPoints: Contact Process manufactures H2SO4
Catalyst: V2O5 (Vanadium Pentoxide)
SO2 + O2 → SO3 → H2SO4 (final product)

subject: Chemistry
text: Rita was given an unknown salt for identification. To the first part, she added a few drops of ammonium hydroxide and obtained a reddish-brown precipitate. To the second part, she added silver nitrate solution and obtained a white precipitate. Name: (a) the cation present and (b) the anion present in the salt.
modelAnswer: (a) Cation: Fe3+ (ferric ion). Reddish-brown precipitate with NH4OH confirms Fe(OH)3 formation. (b) Anion: Cl- (chloride ion). White precipitate with AgNO3 that is insoluble in dilute HNO3 confirms AgCl.
keyPoints: Fe3+ + 3NH4OH → Fe(OH)3 (reddish-brown ppt)
Cl- + AgNO3 → AgCl (white ppt, insoluble in HNO3)
Salt is FeCl3 (ferric chloride)

subject: Chemistry
text: Calcium carbonate reacts with dilute HCl: CaCO3 + 2HCl → CaCl2 + H2O + CO2. (a) What is the mass of 5 moles of CaCO3? (Relative molecular mass = 100) (b) How many moles of HCl will react with 5 moles of CaCO3? (c) What volume of CO2 is liberated at STP?
modelAnswer: (a) Mass = 5 × 100 = 500 g. (b) From equation: 1 mole CaCO3 reacts with 2 moles HCl, so 5 moles CaCO3 reacts with 10 moles HCl. (c) 1 mole gas at STP = 22.4 L; 5 moles CO2 = 5 × 22.4 = 112 L.
keyPoints: Mass = moles × molar mass = 5 × 100 = 500 g
Moles HCl = 2 × moles CaCO3 = 10 moles
Volume CO2 at STP = 5 × 22.4 = 112 L

subject: Chemistry
text: Choose the organic compound from the list — Ethene, Ethanoic acid, Ethanol, Methanal — to answer: (a) The compound which does not have a double bond in its structure. (b) The compound which in its pure form turns into an ice-like solid on cooling. (c) The compound which is used for artificial ripening of fruits.
modelAnswer: (a) Ethanol (C2H5OH) — it has only single bonds, no double bond. (b) Ethanoic acid (glacial acetic acid) — it freezes to an ice-like solid at 16.6°C. (c) Ethene (C2H4) — it is the plant hormone used commercially for artificial ripening of fruits.
keyPoints: Ethanol: no double bond (single bonds only)
Ethanoic acid: glacial form solidifies at 16.6°C
Ethene: used for artificial ripening of fruits

subject: Chemistry
text: Give reasons for the following: (a) Inert gases do not form ions. (b) Covalent compounds have a low melting and boiling point.
modelAnswer: (a) Inert gases have completely filled outermost shells (stable octet/duplet configuration), so they have very high ionization energy and zero electron affinity — they neither lose nor gain electrons easily. (b) Covalent compounds are molecular; intermolecular forces (van der Waals) between molecules are very weak, so little energy is needed to separate molecules, giving low melting/boiling points.
keyPoints: Inert gases: stable electronic configuration → no tendency to gain/lose e-
Covalent compounds: weak van der Waals forces between molecules
Low energy needed to separate molecules → low melting/boiling points

subject: Chemistry
text: Arrange the following as per the instructions given: (a) Carbon, Fluorine, Beryllium — in decreasing order of atomic size. (b) Sulphuric acid, Phosphoric acid, Acetic acid — in increasing order of number of replaceable H atoms per molecule. (c) Potassium, Lithium, Sodium — in increasing order of ionization potential.
modelAnswer: (a) Atomic size decreases across a period; Be > C > F (decreasing atomic size). (b) Acetic acid (1 H), Sulphuric acid (2 H), Phosphoric acid (3 H) — increasing order: Acetic acid < Sulphuric acid < Phosphoric acid. (c) Ionization potential increases up the group; K < Na < Li (increasing ionization potential).
keyPoints: Atomic size decreases across period: Be > C > F
Replaceable H: CH3COOH=1, H2SO4=2, H3PO4=3
IP increases up group: K < Na < Li

subject: Chemistry
text: Define the following terms: (a) Molar volume (b) Normal salt
modelAnswer: (a) Molar volume: The volume occupied by one mole (6.022 × 10²³ molecules) of any gas at STP (Standard Temperature and Pressure), which equals 22.4 litres. (b) Normal salt: A salt formed by the complete replacement of all ionisable hydrogen atoms of an acid by a metal or ammonium ion, e.g., NaCl, Na2SO4.
keyPoints: Molar volume = 22.4 L at STP for any gas
Normal salt: complete replacement of all H atoms of acid
Examples: NaCl, Na2SO4, KCl

subject: Chemistry
text: Complete and balance the following equations: (a) Al2O3 + NaOH → (b) C2H5COONa + NaOH → (with CaO, Δ) (c) C2H4Br2 + alcoholic KOH →
modelAnswer: (a) Al2O3 + 2NaOH → 2NaAlO2 + H2O (Sodium aluminate + water) (b) C2H5COONa + NaOH → C2H6 + Na2CO3 (Propane + sodium carbonate — decarboxylation with CaO/Δ) (c) C2H4Br2 + 2KOH(alc) → CH≡CH + 2KBr + 2H2O (Ethyne formed by double dehydrohalogenation)
keyPoints: Al2O3 + 2NaOH → 2NaAlO2 + H2O (amphoteric oxide)
Decarboxylation: RCOONa + NaOH → R-H + Na2CO3
Double dehydrohalogenation of dihalide gives alkyne

subject: Chemistry
text: During the electrolysis of CuSO4 solution with copper electrodes: (a) What happens at the anode? (b) Does the concentration of CuSO4 solution change? Give reason.
modelAnswer: (a) At the anode (copper), oxidation occurs: Cu → Cu2+ + 2e−. The copper anode dissolves into the solution. (b) The concentration of CuSO4 does NOT change because Cu2+ ions deposited at cathode are exactly replenished by Cu2+ ions entering from the dissolving anode, maintaining constant concentration.
keyPoints: Anode: Cu dissolves → Cu2+ + 2e−
Cathode: Cu2+ + 2e− → Cu (copper deposited)
Concentration unchanged: loss at cathode = gain from anode

subject: Chemistry
text: Arrange the following in order as instructed: (a) Na, Mg, Al — decreasing order of atomic size. (b) HF, HCl, HBr — increasing order of bond strength. (c) Li, Na, K — increasing order of reactivity with water.
modelAnswer: (a) Atomic size decreases across period: Na > Mg > Al. (b) Bond strength decreases down group; HF has shortest, strongest bond: HBr < HCl < HF (increasing bond strength). (c) Reactivity with water increases down Group 1: Li < Na < K.
keyPoints: Atomic size decreases left to right across period
Bond strength: HF > HCl > HBr (shorter bond = stronger)
Group 1 reactivity increases down the group: Li < Na < K

subject: Chemistry
text: Identify the organic compound: (a) Homologous series with general formula CnH2n. Name the first member. (b) The organic acid present in vinegar.
modelAnswer: (a) CnH2n is the general formula for alkenes. The first member is Ethene (C2H4) — methene/methylene does not exist as a stable compound. (b) Ethanoic acid (acetic acid, CH3COOH) is the organic acid present in vinegar.
keyPoints: CnH2n = alkenes; first member = ethene (n=2)
Vinegar contains 4-8% ethanoic acid (acetic acid)
Methane (CH4) follows CnH2n+2 (alkanes)

subject: Chemistry
text: Identify the salt formed and state whether it is acidic, basic or normal: (a) Excess HCl + NaOH (b) NaOH + H3PO4 in 1:1 molar ratio (c) NH4OH + H2SO4 (excess acid)
modelAnswer: (a) NaCl — normal salt (both H completely replaced, formed from strong acid + strong base). (b) NaH2PO4 — acid salt (only one H of H3PO4 replaced in 1:1 ratio, two replaceable H remain). (c) (NH4)2SO4 — normal salt if stoichiometric, but if excess H2SO4 then NH4HSO4 (acid salt).
keyPoints: NaOH + HCl → NaCl (normal salt)
1:1 NaOH + H3PO4 → NaH2PO4 (acid salt, 2 H remain)
Acid salt: partial replacement of H atoms

subject: Chemistry
text: Draw the electron dot (Lewis) structure of: (a) Ammonia (NH3) and (b) Carbon dioxide (CO2). [Atomic numbers: N=7, C=6, O=8, H=1]
modelAnswer: (a) NH3: Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons; shares 1 each with 3 H atoms forming 3 N-H bonds. One lone pair remains on N. Structure shows N at centre with 3 H atoms and 1 lone pair. (b) CO2: Carbon has 4 valence electrons; shares 2 each with two O atoms forming 2 double bonds. Each O has 2 lone pairs. Linear structure: O=C=O.
keyPoints: NH3: 3 bond pairs + 1 lone pair on N; pyramidal shape
CO2: 2 double bonds (C=O), 2 lone pairs on each O; linear
Lone pairs shown as dots, bond pairs as lines or pairs of dots

subject: Chemistry
text: Give reasons for: (a) Aluminium is extracted by electrolytic reduction and not by carbon reduction. (b) Zinc is refined by distillation. (c) Copper is purified by electrolytic refining.
modelAnswer: (a) Al is a very reactive metal (above C in activity series); carbon cannot reduce Al2O3 at practical temperatures. Also, Al forms Al4C3 (aluminum carbide) with carbon, making the product impure. (b) Zinc has a low boiling point (907°C) and vaporises easily; distillation separates it from less volatile impurities — Zn vapours are collected and condensed. (c) Copper is refined electrolytically because it is a good conductor; impure copper at anode dissolves and pure copper deposits at cathode selectively.
keyPoints: Al more reactive than C; cannot be reduced by carbon
Zn: low boiling point → distillation suitable
Cu electrolytic refining: impure anode dissolves, pure Cu deposits at cathode

subject: Chemistry
text: Identify the gas evolved in each case: (a) Copper is treated with concentrated nitric acid. (b) Ammonium chloride solution is treated with sodium hydroxide solution and warmed.
modelAnswer: (a) Brown/reddish-brown gas NO2 (nitrogen dioxide) is evolved. Cu + 4HNO3(conc.) → Cu(NO3)2 + 2NO2 + 2H2O. (b) Ammonia (NH3) gas is evolved with a pungent smell. NH4Cl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O + NH3.
keyPoints: Cu + conc. HNO3 → NO2 (brown gas)
NH4Cl + NaOH(warm) → NH3 (pungent, turns moist red litmus blue)
Test NH3: moist red litmus turns blue

subject: Chemistry
text: Write the electrode reactions for the electrolysis of acidulated water (dilute H2SO4): (a) at the cathode (b) at the anode. Also, what is the ratio of volumes of gases collected at cathode and anode?
modelAnswer: (a) Cathode (reduction): 2H+ + 2e− → H2. Hydrogen gas is liberated. (b) Anode (oxidation): 2H2O → O2 + 4H+ + 4e− (or 4OH− → 2H2O + O2 + 4e−). Oxygen gas is liberated. Ratio of volumes: H2 : O2 = 2 : 1 (by volume, as 4 H+ give 2H2 but only 1 O2 per 4 electrons at anode).
keyPoints: Cathode: 2H+ + 2e− → H2 (reduction)
Anode: 2H2O → O2 + 4H+ + 4e− (oxidation)
Volume ratio H2 : O2 = 2 : 1

subject: Chemistry
text: Differentiate between Alkanes and Alkenes based on: (a) general formula (b) type of reaction they undergo.
modelAnswer: (a) Alkanes: CnH2n+2 (saturated); Alkenes: CnH2n (unsaturated, one double bond). (b) Alkanes undergo substitution reactions (e.g., halogenation in presence of UV light). Alkenes undergo addition reactions (e.g., with H2, Br2, HBr) due to the C=C double bond.
keyPoints: Alkanes: CnH2n+2, saturated, substitution reactions
Alkenes: CnH2n, unsaturated (C=C), addition reactions
Double bond makes alkenes more reactive than alkanes

subject: Chemistry
text: Element X has atomic number 17. (a) Which period does X belong to? (b) Which group does X belong to? (c) Is X a metal or non-metal? Give reason.
modelAnswer: (a) Electronic configuration of X (Cl): 2, 8, 7 — 3 shells → Period 3. (b) 7 electrons in outermost shell → Group 17 (Halogens). (c) Non-metal — it has 7 valence electrons, needs only 1 more to complete octet; it has high electronegativity and tends to gain electrons rather than lose them.
keyPoints: Cl (Z=17): configuration 2,8,7
3 shells → Period 3; 7 valence e- → Group 17
Non-metal: gains electrons, high electronegativity

subject: Chemistry
text: During electroplating of an iron cup with nickel: (a) Why is the iron cup placed at the cathode? (b) Name the ion that must be present in the electrolyte.
modelAnswer: (a) The iron cup is placed at the cathode because cations (Ni2+) from the electrolyte migrate to the cathode where they are reduced and deposited as nickel metal on the iron cup (object to be plated always placed at cathode). (b) Ni2+ (nickel ions) must be present in the electrolyte (nickel sulphate or nickel ammonium sulphate solution).
keyPoints: Cathode: reduction occurs; Ni2+ + 2e− → Ni deposited on cup
Object to be plated always placed at cathode
Electrolyte must contain Ni2+ ions (NiSO4 solution)

subject: Chemistry
text: Rewrite the following statements by adding the correct word: (a) Sulphuric acid acts as a dehydrating agent. (b) Ammonia reacts with chlorine to give ammonium chloride and nitrogen.
modelAnswer: (a) Concentrated sulphuric acid acts as a dehydrating agent. (b) Excess ammonia reacts with chlorine to give ammonium chloride and nitrogen: 8NH3 + 3Cl2 → 6NH4Cl + N2.
keyPoints: Concentrated H2SO4 is the dehydrating agent (dilute does not)
Excess NH3 + Cl2 → NH4Cl + N2 (NH3 acts as reducing agent)
Ammonia also reduces CuO to Cu (reducing property)

subject: Chemistry
text: Calculate: (a) the number of moles in 36 g of water. (b) the number of molecules in 0.5 moles of CO2. [H=1, O=16]
modelAnswer: (a) Molar mass of H2O = 2+16 = 18 g/mol. Moles = 36/18 = 2 moles. (b) Molecules = 0.5 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 3.011 × 10²³ molecules.
keyPoints: Moles = mass / molar mass = 36/18 = 2 mol
Molecules = moles × Avogadro's number
0.5 mol CO2 = 3.011 × 10²³ molecules

subject: Chemistry
text: Give IUPAC names for: (a) CH3-CH2-CH2-OH (b) CH3-CO-CH3 (c) CH3-CH2-COOH
modelAnswer: (a) CH3CH2CH2OH — Propan-1-ol (3 carbons, OH at C1, suffix -ol). (b) CH3COCH3 — Propan-2-one / Acetone (3 carbons, ketone at C2, suffix -one). (c) CH3CH2COOH — Propanoic acid (3 carbons, carboxylic acid at C1, suffix -oic acid).
keyPoints: Propan-1-ol: 3C + OH at position 1
Propan-2-one (acetone): 3C + C=O at position 2
Propanoic acid: 3C + COOH (carboxylic acid)

subject: Chemistry
text: Name the main metal used in making: (a) Duralumin (b) Stainless steel. Name one use of each alloy.
modelAnswer: (a) Duralumin: main metal is Aluminium (Al). It is used in making aircraft bodies and spacecraft due to its lightness and strength. (b) Stainless steel: main metal is Iron (Fe). It is used for making surgical instruments, kitchen utensils, and cutlery.
keyPoints: Duralumin: Al + Cu + Mn + Mg; used in aircraft
Stainless steel: Fe + Cr + Ni; used in cutlery/surgical tools
Alloys are harder than pure metals

subject: Chemistry
text: Differentiate between electrovalent (ionic) bond and covalent bond based on: (a) how the bond is formed (b) electrical conductivity of compounds.
modelAnswer: (a) Ionic bond: formed by complete transfer of electrons from one atom to another (metal to non-metal), forming ions. Covalent bond: formed by sharing of electrons between two non-metal atoms. (b) Ionic compounds conduct electricity when dissolved in water or in molten state (ions free to move). Covalent compounds generally do not conduct electricity (no free ions).
keyPoints: Ionic: transfer of electrons → ions form (electrostatic attraction)
Covalent: sharing of electrons (no ions formed)
Ionic compounds conduct electricity in solution/molten; covalent do not

subject: Chemistry
text: The electrolysis of acidulated water is carried out using platinum electrodes. (a) Name the gases collected at the anode and cathode. (b) In what volume ratio are the gases collected? (c) Write the ionic equation for the reaction at the anode.
modelAnswer: (a) Cathode: Hydrogen (H2); Anode: Oxygen (O2). (b) Ratio cathode:anode = 2:1 by volume (2 volumes of H2 for every 1 volume of O2). (c) Anode (oxidation): 4OH⁻ → 2H2O + O2 + 4e⁻ (or 2H2O → O2 + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻).
keyPoints: Cathode: H2 (reduction); Anode: O2 (oxidation)
Volume ratio H2:O2 = 2:1
Anode ionic equation: 4OH⁻ → 2H2O + O2 + 4e⁻

subject: Chemistry
text: Give reasons: (a) Sulphuric acid is called a dibasic acid. (b) Hydrochloric acid is not used in the preparation of lead sulphate.
modelAnswer: (a) Sulphuric acid (H2SO4) has two replaceable hydrogen atoms per molecule that can be replaced by a metal to form salts — hence dibasic (diprotic). It can form two series of salts: normal (Na2SO4) and acid (NaHSO4). (b) HCl is not used because lead sulphate (PbSO4) is insoluble. Mixing HCl with lead sulphate or lead compounds would give PbCl2, not PbSO4. Instead, dilute H2SO4 is used for PbSO4 preparation.
keyPoints: Dibasic: 2 replaceable H atoms per molecule → two salt series
HCl cannot give sulphate ion (SO4²⁻); produces chloride instead
PbSO4 made from Pb compound + dilute H2SO4

subject: Chemistry
text: Write the structural formula of: (a) Ethanol (b) Ethanoic acid (c) State one difference between the two compounds based on their reaction with sodium metal.
modelAnswer: (a) Ethanol: CH3-CH2-OH (C2H5OH). (b) Ethanoic acid: CH3-COOH. (c) Difference: Both react with sodium metal to produce hydrogen gas. Ethanol: 2C2H5OH + 2Na → 2C2H5ONa + H2 (slowly). Ethanoic acid: 2CH3COOH + 2Na → 2CH3COONa + H2 (more vigorously, as it is acidic and the reaction is faster).
keyPoints: Ethanol: C2H5OH; Ethanoic acid: CH3COOH
Both react with Na to give H2
Ethanoic acid reacts more vigorously (acidic); ethanol reacts slowly

subject: Chemistry
text: Draw the electron dot structure of: (a) Hydrogen chloride (HCl) (b) Chlorine (Cl2). [Atomic number: H=1, Cl=17]
modelAnswer: (a) HCl: Chlorine has 7 valence electrons (configuration 2,8,7); shares 1 with H's 1 electron → one shared pair (covalent bond), 3 lone pairs on Cl. (b) Cl2: Each Cl has 7 valence electrons; they share 1 electron each → one shared pair (single bond), 3 lone pairs on each Cl. Both are covalent molecules.
keyPoints: HCl: 1 bond pair + 3 lone pairs on Cl; H has no lone pairs
Cl2: 1 bond pair + 3 lone pairs on each Cl
Both covalent; Cl has 7 valence electrons (group 17)

subject: Chemistry
text: Identify the salt and write the equation for its preparation by: (a) Direct combination — Iron with chlorine. (b) Displacement — Iron displacing copper from copper sulphate. (c) Double decomposition — Lead nitrate with potassium iodide.
modelAnswer: (a) 2Fe + 3Cl2 → 2FeCl3 (iron(III) chloride — ferric chloride; salt = FeCl3). (b) Fe + CuSO4 → FeSO4 + Cu (iron(II) sulphate; salt = FeSO4). (c) Pb(NO3)2 + 2KI → PbI2↓ + 2KNO3 (lead iodide precipitate; salt = PbI2, yellow ppt formed).
keyPoints: Direct combination: 2Fe + 3Cl2 → 2FeCl3
Displacement: Fe + CuSO4 → FeSO4 + Cu
Double decomposition: Pb(NO3)2 + 2KI → PbI2↓ + 2KNO3

subject: Chemistry
text: Identify the element from its electronic configuration: 2, 8, 8, 2. (a) State its period and group. (b) Is it a metal or non-metal? (c) Write the formula of its oxide.
modelAnswer: (a) Configuration 2,8,8,2 = 4 shells → Period 4; 2 electrons in outermost shell → Group 2 (Alkaline Earth Metals). Element = Calcium (Ca, Z=20). (b) Metal — it loses 2 electrons to form Ca²⁺ (electropositive element). (c) Oxide formula: CaO (calcium oxide — basic oxide).
keyPoints: 2,8,8,2: 4 shells → Period 4; 2 valence e⁻ → Group 2 → Calcium
Metal: loses 2e⁻ to form Ca²⁺
Oxide: CaO (basic oxide; reacts with water → Ca(OH)2)

subject: Chemistry
text: Calculate: (a) The number of moles in 11.2 L of CO2 at STP. (b) The mass of 3.011 × 10²³ molecules of O2. [O=16]
modelAnswer: (a) 1 mole gas = 22.4 L at STP. Moles of CO2 = 11.2/22.4 = 0.5 moles. (b) 3.011 × 10²³ molecules = 0.5 moles (since 1 mole = 6.022×10²³). Molar mass of O2 = 32 g. Mass = 0.5 × 32 = 16 g.
keyPoints: Moles = volume/22.4 at STP = 11.2/22.4 = 0.5 mol
3.011×10²³ = 0.5 × Avogadro = 0.5 moles

subject: Chemistry
text: Describe the Hall-Heroult process for the extraction of aluminium. (a) Name the electrolyte and the electrodes used. (b) Write the electrode reactions. (c) Why is cryolite added to alumina?
modelAnswer: (a) Electrolyte: Fused alumina (Al2O3) dissolved in molten cryolite (Na3AlF6) with CaF2. Anode: graphite (carbon); Cathode: steel vessel lined with carbon. (b) Cathode: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al (molten Al sinks to bottom). Anode: 2O²⁻ → O2 + 4e⁻ (oxygen burns carbon anodes). (c) Cryolite is added to lower the melting point of alumina from ~2045°C to ~950°C, making the process economically and practically feasible.
keyPoints: Electrolyte: Al2O3 in molten cryolite + CaF2; graphite electrodes
Cathode: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al; Anode: 2O²⁻ → O2 + 4e⁻
Cryolite: lowers melting point of alumina (2045°C → ~950°C)

subject: Chemistry
text: In a salt analysis experiment: To part A, ammonium hydroxide was added which gave a reddish-brown precipitate. To part B, barium chloride was added giving a white precipitate insoluble in dilute HCl. Identify the cation and anion.
modelAnswer: Cation: Fe³⁺ (ferric ion) — gives reddish-brown precipitate Fe(OH)3 with NH4OH: Fe³⁺ + 3NH4OH → Fe(OH)3↓ (reddish-brown) + 3NH4⁺. Anion: SO4²⁻ (sulphate) — white precipitate with BaCl2 is BaSO4, which is insoluble in dilute HCl: Ba²⁺ + SO4²⁻ → BaSO4↓ (white). Salt = Fe2(SO4)3 (ferric sulphate).
keyPoints: Fe³⁺: reddish-brown ppt Fe(OH)3 with NH4OH
SO4²⁻: white ppt BaSO4 with BaCl2, insoluble in HCl
Salt = Fe2(SO4)3 (ferric sulphate)

subject: Chemistry
text: State what is observed when: (a) ethanol is heated with acidified potassium dichromate. (b) ethanoic acid is added to sodium carbonate solution. (c) ethanol is dehydrated with concentrated H2SO4 at 170°C.
modelAnswer: (a) Ethanol is oxidized — orange K2Cr2O7 turns green (Cr³⁺ formed); ethanol is converted to ethanal then to ethanoic acid (acetic acid). (b) Brisk effervescence of CO2 gas is observed: 2CH3COOH + Na2CO3 → 2CH3COONa + H2O + CO2. (c) Ethanol is dehydrated to ethene (C2H4): C2H5OH → CH2=CH2 + H2O. The product is an unsaturated gas.
keyPoints: Acidified K2Cr2O7: orange → green; ethanol → ethanoic acid (oxidation)
CH3COOH + Na2CO3 → CO2 effervescence (acid-carbonate reaction)
Dehydration (170°C, conc H2SO4): C2H5OH → C2H4 + H2O (alkene formed)
